![Drill 2: 11 personnel under center, the Y in-line on the left, receivers in tight splits (H, the third receiver, and X about 10 yards from the ball); the Z, a slot receiver on the right, goes in jet motion to the left (the dashed arrow ends where he will be at the snap, just behind the quarterback). The defense: a four-man front (a 9 outside the Y, a 3, a 1 and a 5) and two linebackers in the box, a nickel back (NB) who stays outside where the Z started, two cornerbacks and two deep safeties. Nobody follows the motion.](12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree_files/figure-html/fig-predict-2-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-2}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A run.** Count the box: six defenders against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), with both safeties
12 yards deep. That is a [light box](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), and the
system's standing answer to two-high safeties is to run the ball at them. The motion told the quarterback two more
things: nobody ran across with the Z, so the coverage is very likely zone, and the safeties didn't rotate down, so
the box is staying light.

Which way is the play-caller's choice, and both answers are textbook in this family:

- **Wide zone left, toward the motion (or the jet sweep itself, handed to the Z).** The Z is just behind the
  quarterback at the snap and keeps running through the mesh toward the left sideline. He doesn't block anyone;
  he is a threat, and the defender on the left edge has to respect a jet sweep for a beat, which is a beat he
  isn't attacking the run.
- **Fake the jet, wide zone right, away from it.** The fake drags the Will and the nickel back toward the motion
  and thins the right side, where the run is going.

If you said "run," you read the picture; the direction is the bonus question.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3.** First-and-10, a series after the bootleg in Drill 1 went for 22 yards. Same 21-personnel look,
tight end on the left, quarterback under center. The defense has changed two things. It now shows **two** deep
safeties before the snap, and when the Z goes in motion across the formation to the right, one safety spins down
into the box on that side while the other runs to the middle of the field. And the backside end on the right is
no longer chasing: on the last two runs he squeezed down the line, square, with his eyes on the quarterback. The
offense's last two wide-zone runs gained 3 and 2 yards. What should the offense call?

::: {#cell-fig-predict-3 .cell execution_count=17}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off3 = off21(strength="left")
d3 = [q.moved(d=12.5, w=8.5) if q.key == "SS" else (q.moved(d=12.5, w=-8.5) if q.key == "FS" else q)
      for q in bear(s=-1)]
p = Play(off3, d3, los=35, to_go=10)
p.motion("Z", to=(-1.5, 6.6))
p.drop("SS", (5.4, 6.6), label=None)
p.drop("FS", (14.0, 0.0), label=None)
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-9.0, 16.5))
say(f, p, 9.0, 10.6, "spins down\non the motion", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 14.0, -4.6, "rotates to\nthe middle", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -3.4, 9.2, "squeezes,\neyes on the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

![Drill 3: the same 21-personnel look, the Z in motion across to the right (dashed blue). Before the snap the defense shows two deep safeties; as the Z moves, the right-side safety spins down into the box and the other rotates to the deep middle (dashed orange), leaving eight in the box and one deep safety still moving at the snap. The backside end (ringed) squeezes with his eyes on the quarterback.](12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree_files/figure-html/fig-predict-3-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-3}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A play-action shot from under center, with max protection: two deep routes against the one safety.** Put
the two changes together. The naked boot is off the table, because the end who used to chase is squeezing and
would be waiting for the quarterback. Wide zone is running into eight in the box, which is what the spin was
for. But the spin has a price: one safety is left to cover the whole deep field, and at the snap he is still
running to the middle. That is the picture the
[yankee](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yankee) concept from
[04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) is built for: fake wide zone, keep the
fullback and the back in to protect, and send two receivers deep, a post from one side and a deep over from the
other. The linebackers and the safety who came down step up for the fake; the lone deep safety can take only one
of the two routes, and the quarterback throws the other.

*Why not the protected boot?* It's a fine safe call, and a good one on second-and-long. But it attacks the short
and middle areas the eight-man box is already crowding; on first-and-10 with one deep safety still moving, the
shot is the bigger reward. This back-and-forth, base play, constraint, a new answer, a new constraint, is
[sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd), and it is how a Shanahan
play-caller spends a game.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Two problems, one family.** Gibbs's and Mike Shanahan's 1990s Broncos built wide zone and the bootleg to block
  defenses that never stood still; Kyle Shanahan's 2017 49ers added the fullback, motion and YAC passing to beat
  fast, light defenses without a star quarterback.
- **Four ingredients, one picture.** Wide zone moves the defense sideways, the fullback forces a personnel choice,
  motion makes the defense answer first, and YAC passes throw into the space all of that empties. The same few
  looks carry all of it.
- **Leave a man free on purpose, then punish him.** Against a bear front the offense can't block everyone, so it
  leaves the backside end and beats him with the bootleg-keeper when he crashes; when he squeezes, the cutback,
  split zone and the protected boot are waiting. The defense's answer to the base play sets up the constraint play.
- **The system raises the quarterback's floor, and the ceiling is still argued.** Several quarterbacks were much
  more efficient inside the family than outside it; even the 49ers' third-and-long success is designed. Goff
  thrived in a cousin offense in Detroit, and EPA can't see the difference McVay paid for in Stafford: the
  plays after the design breaks are a coach's judgment, not a number.
- **The fingerprint:** under center and in motion, 21 or heavy personnel (49ers), play-action at the top of the
  league (Rams), and receivers who gain far more after the catch than the catch predicts. From 2019 to 2025 the
  49ers were first in YAC over expected by a wide margin and top ten in EPA per play in six of seven seasons.
- **Label every staff by season.** In 2025 the family's first generation called plays in San Francisco, Los
  Angeles, Green Bay, Miami and Seattle (Super Bowl LX champions), with McVay's former assistants calling them in
  Minnesota, Jacksonville, Cincinnati, Atlanta and Houston. In 2026 Kubiak (Las Vegas) and Mike LaFleur (Arizona)
  are head coaches who call plays, McDaniel calls the Chargers' plays, Fleury Seattle's, Slowik coordinates Miami's
  offense and Stefanski is Atlanta's head coach.

Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015) and his Grantland piece on Gary Kubiak's Houston run game
(2012) are the best short introductions to the Gibbs zone system. Alex Gibbs's own clinic video, "Outside Zone,
Tight Zone, Boots and Thoughts on the Power," is still sold to coaches. Robert Mays's film writing and podcasts at The
Ringer cover the modern Shanahan and McVay versions in detail. For the data,
nflverse's play-by-play carries the expected-YAC columns used here, and Next Gen Stats publishes receiver YAC over
expected on its website; [Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)
shows how to build an expected-YAC model of your own from tracking data.
:::
